identity.title: Differences between the Pokémon games and animated series

leadText: The Pokémon animated series often differs from the Pokémon games. While the games tend to dictate the venues and main events that occur within the animated series, and tend to correspond on basic information, there are many noticeable differences or contradictions that can be seen between the two media.
plainText:
The Pokémon animated series often differs from the Pokémon games. While the games tend to dictate the venues and main events that occur within the animated series, and tend to correspond on basic information, there are many noticeable differences or contradictions that can be seen between the two media.

==Most notable differences==
===Pokémon===
====Coloration====
 in Pokémon the Series]]
 
 differ in various ways between the and . Pokémon with different colors from their normal or ones appear, though Pokémon with the official Shiny colors do appear as well. 

====Cries====
The cries of Pokémon in the core series games differ significantly from the cries in the animated series. An exception is in and from Generation VI to , as well as in and in Generation VIII, both of which actually say their names when interacted with or when called into . Both Pokémon, as well as , also have unique cries for their Gigantamax forms.

====Population of Legendary and Mythical Pokémon====
 
Multiples of various species of and Mythical Pokémon are sighted throughout the series. In the games, usually only one can be found per game, though it is implied that more exist. Legendary and Mythical Pokémon are also able to in the animated series, contrary to the core series games. 

====Pokédex records====
The Pokédex can show the data of any in the animated series without needing it to be first.

====Pokémon Eggs====
Pokémon Eggs have a different appearance depending on the Pokémon species that is inside of the Egg, although in Pokémon Journeys: The Series, the design is more standardized to match the appearance of Eggs in the games, with only the color of the spots differing between species.

====Evolution====
Pokémon have the right to decide if they want to evolve, and can choose if they don't want to evolve. However, in the games, the Pokémon only evolves if and when the player wants it to and the requirements have been met. Notable examples are Ash's Pikachu and , of , and Dawn's Piplup. The exceptions are and , where the Pokémon the player receives from Oak (the player's Pikachu or , respectively) refuses to evolve.

In the games, evolutionary methods revolving around leveling up usually occur after a battle, while in the animated series, Evolution can occur during a battle or a serious situation. One example is when 's Chikorita evolved into to protect him from . Trade Evolution also seems to function somewhat differently than in the games. For example, in the episode Outrageous Fortunes, Misty's Poliwhirl evolved into while being transferred between two Pokémon Centers rather than from another Trainer. Stone-induced Evolution also seems to be somewhat inconsistent. For example, in The Battling Eevee Brothers, a Trainer's evolves into immediately after making physical contact with a Water Stone; however, in a previous episode, Ash's Pikachu makes physical contact with a Thunder Stone, but does not evolve.

===Battling and moves===
====Battle dynamics and rules====
In the , Pokémon battles take place in real-time as opposed to being turn-based. This means that Pokémon Trainers are not forced to wait for the other to make a move. However, most Trainers usually wait for the opponent to finish issuing commands. Additionally, Trainers (particularly ) often use improvised moves and techniques that are not possible in the . For example, moves can be used together to make a totally new move, or a move can be rendered harmless in an unorthodox way, such as in Sky High Gym Battle!, when Winona's Pelipper used to attract Ash's Pikachu's electricity and divert it into the ground to render it useless. Trainers can also order their Pokémon to dodge attacks, regardless of the accuracy of that move in the games, though starting from Generation VI, Pokémon with high affection can occasionally dodge moves that would usually hit. Furthermore, moves that normally cannot miss in the games, such as , , and , can still occasionally miss in the animated series. Notably, introduces real-time battle mechanics much more reminiscent of the animated series, with Pokémon no longer having to take turns in battle and Pokémon being able to dodge each other's attacks by moving out of the way while following their Trainer.

All official Pokémon Trainer battles in the animated series have a judge, who sets the rules and referees the battle, and is able to declare when a Pokémon is unable to battle, which would eliminate that Pokémon from the match. In the games, however, aside from a battle facility match, any Pokémon that has fainted can be revived and used again in battle as long as the Trainer has at least one Pokémon left.

====Disobedience====
Some Pokémon that have been recently caught or evolved may disobey their Trainer until that Trainer is able to find a way to get through to them, with the prime example being Ash's Charizard. In most core series games, only traded Pokémon disobey their Trainer until Badges that can neutralize this problem are acquired. Some later games without Gym Badges have their own method to increase obedience rank. However, in , any Pokémon may disobey their Trainer prior to fulfilling the obedience requirement; starting with , only Pokémon obtained or caught at too high a level will be disobedient.

====Move mechanics====
Pokémon can have more than four moves in the animated series, and are not required to forget an old move in order to learn a new one (although some of the moves a Pokémon is shown using when first introduced will generally fall into disuse as the Pokémon learns more powerful moves as the series continues). Later series are usually more likely to have Pokémon stick to the four-move limit, however.

Additionally, the concept of physical and special moves is rarely mentioned in the animated series.

PP also does not seem to exist in the animated series. However, like people, Pokémon can be worn out from constant battling and eventually collapse from exhaustion. Although, in the games, a Pokémon that runs out of PP in every move can faint from the recoil damage of .

TMs do not seem to exist either. Instead, TM-exclusive moves must be taught to the Pokémon over a period of time. Additionally, HM moves are shown as regular moves; they are not used as tools for certain situations like in the games. Instead, Pokémon's natural abilities or moves can be used to similar effect, such as characters riding on the back of to cross bodies of water akin to , or using moves such as to cut down trees or vines like the move .

Furthermore, Egg Moves, which a Pokémon knows upon hatching in the games, are able to be picked up naturally as the Pokémon grows (one example being Ash's Pikachu learning 424 episodes after its first appearance).

====Move errors and discrepancies====
Pokémon can sometimes use a move that normally would not affect the target in the games, notably with , who has been able to affect s with Electric attacks, which it cannot do in the games.

 
Occasionally, the animated series also shows Pokémon using moves they cannot learn in the games. However, some of these cases may be attributed to a translation error or a misinterpretation. Examples include telling Pikachu to use "electric attack" when he could just mean to use an electric attack, or Pokémon using basic attacks like or simply because they are just basic attacks.

There have also been cases where move or status mechanics have been ignored or altered in the animated series that contradicts the games. One example of this is causing recoil damage when blocked with instead of being caused from a small amount based on the damage inflicted. Another example is poisoning Ash's Pokémon when they touched the ground instead of when they were switched out. This affected his and , which would be immune to the move in the games due to being types. However, the animated series sometimes contradicts its own rules. For example, when Ash asks his to dodge and counter with when it's been explained before that the Pokémon needs to concentrate a moment without being disturbed to be able to use the attack.

Move effects differ as well. For example, acts more like and does direct damage, whereas in the games it only inflicts a . and deal direct damage in the game but in the animated series it has a psychokinesis-like effect, able to move the target to the user's will. puts a Pokémon to sleep in game, but in the animated series, while it can be used to inflict sleep, it also has effects similar to the alleged effects of real-life - putting the target into a trance or suggestible state.

===Pokémon League===
In the , there can be more than the eight usual Gyms in each region. However, only ever faces the ones from the , with the others challenged by his rivals. For example, in The Battle of the Badge, Gary Oak is seen with ten badges prior to trying to obtain an Earth Badge, and, of those ten badges, only three are from Gyms found in the games, implying that the Kanto region has at least 15 Gyms in the animated series.

Official Gym and League battles also set limits on how many a can use to fight with, whereas in the games, only facilities like the Battle Tower set limits.

All Trainers who collect at least eight Badges compete in a Pokémon League Conference. In the games, only Trainers who manage to collect all the specific regional Badges are qualified to challenge the Elite Four and the current . In the animated series, Trainers may directly challenge the current Champion without additional requirements, as seen with several of 's battles.

===Contests===
 
In the , Pokémon Contest rounds work very differently. In the first one, called the Performance Stage, s display an array of moves and skills to showcase their , while in the , the player simply presents their Pokémon so its condition can be evaluated. The second round is different as well. In the animated series, contestants face each other in a Contest Battle, while in the games all the participants take turns showing off one move at a time.

===Locations===
Locations are not all the same between the and the . Multiple locations are added to regions to carry out plots in the animated series, and in addition to the core series regions, there are two regions exclusive to the animated series: the Orange Islands and the Decolore Islands. 

Some towns and other locations are also depicted differently in the animated series compared to the games. For example, the Whirl Islands are shown to be populated, but in the games they are just a series of caves. Littleroot Town is shown to be a coastal town, while in the games it is surrounded by woodland on all sides. Additionally, Ultra Ruin in the animated series is an alternate dimension of Alola, rather than a part of Ultra Space.

===Pokémon Centers===
Pokémon Centers in the animated series function somewhat differently from their in-game counterparts: in the games, Pokémon Centers restore a Pokémon to full health in a matter of seconds regardless of the severity of its injuries, and can do so while the Pokémon remains inside its Poké Ball; in the animated series, Pokémon Centers are often shown to require varying amounts of time to heal a Pokémon depending on the severity of its injuries, ranging from a few moments to several hours, and may or may not require the Pokémon to be out of its Poké Ball, depending on the individual Pokémon Center. Additionally, Pokémon Centers in the animated series are shown to function similarly to , offering overnight housing to Trainers.
